notes:
SOURCES. Two read-only Kaggle CLI calls ('competitions list --category all --sort-by latestDeadline -v', pages 1 and 2; page 2 contains only ended competitions plus PS S6E9). Chrome, in one new tab that has since been closed: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions; https://www.kaggle.com/competitions?listOption=active (2 pages); the Community+Active filter (9 pages, almost all classroom Kudos contests, not listed individually); the Community+Monetary filter (2 pages, listed above); the Medals+Active filter (https://www.kaggle.com/competitions?listOption=active&prestigeFilter=medals); and the overview pages for Enveda, RSNA Knee, Gemma-4 Agent, ARC-AGI-3 and ARC-AGI-2. Nothing was clicked apart from the filter chips. No Join, Submit or rules buttons were touched.

UPCOMING. The site has no 'Upcoming/Launching soon' filter; the status filters are only Active/Entered/Completed/Spotlight. No announced future competition is visible anywhere. The only expected launch is Playground S6E10 around 1 Oct. That is an estimate from the monthly cadence, and it gives no medals.

MEDALS. The Medals filter shows exactly 6 active competitions: Gemma-4 Developer Agent, Enveda CASMI, RSNA Knee, Kaggriculture (closes today), ARC-AGI-3 and ARC-AGI-2. The hackathon or paper tracks, Playground, Getting Started and all Community contests do not award medals. Days-left figures for Community contests are estimates taken from the site's relative wording.

RECOMMENDATION (my judgement, i.e. estimates).
1) MAIN PICK: Enveda CASMI 2026. It has the longest runway: 75 days, entry deadline 7 Dec, started 14 Sep, so we are only about 2 weeks behind. 1,857 teams is a moderate field, so the bronze cut is roughly the top 10%, about rank 185 (estimate). The usual winning structure fits our constraints well. It is candidate generation (formula from precursor m/z, retrieval of candidates from public structure databases, which the rules allow as external data) plus a learned ranker (spectrum-to-fingerprint or GBDT/small-MLP reranker trained on public spectral libraries). That work is mostly CPU plus one-off Kaggle GPU runs, not a 60-150 GPU-h detector. The metric (MRR@25 over InChIKey14) can be computed locally, so we can build an honest held-out CV in the first days. We can hold it out by scaffold or molecule to guard against the public/private shrink. Biology and chemistry is also close to our Biohub domain. Risk: domain ramp-up (MS/MS, RDKit), and possible dependence on large public libraries that must be packaged into a no-internet 9 h notebook.
2) OPTIONAL SECOND: Gemma-4 Developer Agent, 63 days, entry deadline 25 Nov. The submission can be just agent.yaml, prompts and skills; LoRA is optional. So a prompt/tool/skill-engineering path needs no training GPU, and Claude Code is strong at exactly this kind of work. Downsides: 1,036 teams of likely strong LLM people; submission rate limits and scoring runtime (12 h harness) make feedback slow; real gains probably need LoRA/RL on a 31B model, which is beyond our GPU budget. Treat it as a learning track with a small medal chance (estimate), or enter only if Enveda turns out blocked.
SKIP: RSNA Knee (22 days, entry 15 Oct; 3D MRI with 4,618 teams and a mature leaderboard needs heavy GPU training, which is exactly our failure mode); ARC-AGI-2/3 (33 days, extremely hard, the leaderboard is dominated by specialists, RTX-pool compute); Kaggriculture and PS S6E9 (close today). Community contests give no medals; Solar Filament ($3k, 779 teams) or UMUD are only worth it for learning or money.
Team note: since the teammates were unreliable, plan Enveda as a solo-capable, CPU-first pipeline. Treat teammate GPUs as a bonus, not a dependency. Team merges are allowed until 7 Dec.

pages.task: For each unknown molecule (1-16 LC-MS/MS spectra per molecule, median 3), predict up to 25 ranked 2D structures as SMILES. Tabular/array data: peak m/z and intensity arrays plus precursor m/z, adduct, collision energy. Test set is about 1,500 spectra of about 400 molecules, all from a Bruker timsTOF. Three hidden novelty classes: (1) in public spectral libraries, reachable by spectral similarity; (2) in PubChem or COCONUT but with no public spectra, reachable by database retrieval; (3) novel structures that must be generated de novo. The class mix is hidden. Train set: about 2.5M spectra covering about 275k structures from 11 libraries. Only enveda-180 (1.15M spectra, but drug-like synthetic chemistry) and enveda-np-examples (1,151 spectra, 250 natural products) are instrument-matched. Source: /data page.
pages.submission: Code competition. CPU notebook <=9 h, GPU notebook <=9 h, internet disabled. Freely and publicly available external data and pretrained models are allowed (for example PubChem/COCONUT candidate lists, MassBank, GeMS/DreaMS pretrained embeddings, SIRIUS/MIST-CF). Output is submission.csv. Source: /overview 'Code Requirements'. Daily submission limit not checked.

pages.notes: The public notebook ceiling (0.386) sits at about LB rank 30-35 of 1,857, with a very flat plateau at 0.383-0.40 from rank 10 to rank 49. Bronze for 1,857 teams is roughly the top 10% (about rank 186) and silver roughly the top 5% (about rank 93) (estimate from Kaggle medal rules). The bronze cutoff is probably below the current public-notebook score, but many forkers will crowd there, and the public LB has only about 130 molecules, so it is noisy. The gap to #1 (+0.08) suggests real signal from own work: database retrieval for class 2, de novo generation for class 3, and timsTOF domain adaptation. The main work is CPU-friendly: spectral similarity, formula prediction, candidate retrieval plus a ranker trained with gradient boosting or a small head. Pretrained DreaMS embeddings allowed. About 75 days left. There is a natural honest CV: hold out structures by scaffold or library, using enveda-np-examples as the instrument-matched validation set. Data is 3 GB, laptop-feasible. Assessment (estimate): best fit to our constraints.

Kaggle runs it with a 12 h agent budget for all tasks, excluding patch validation. The only tools are those provided by the harness. Max 1 submission per day; team size up to 5 (/rules). External data and models are allowed unless prohibited by the host (/rules section 6). Training a LoRA for a 31B model is up to the team, on its own compute.

compute_need: Every serious agent runs a local LLM of 27-31B parameters. Source: arcprize.org/blog/arc-prize-2026-milestone-1. Milestone 1 went to Tufa Labs "The Duck" (Qwen 3.6 27B FP8, which writes and runs Python in a REPL). 2nd and 3rd place both used Gemma-4-31B as a vision LLM returning JSON actions. Each full evaluation is a notebook run of up to 9 h on the RTX 6000 (g4-standard-48) or a Kaggle GPU (/overview). Whether those runs count against our ~30 GPU-h/week is unverified. If they do, we get about 3 evaluation runs a week (estimate). Development cannot run on the laptop CPU: a 27B FP8 model needs about 28-30 GB of VRAM (estimate). The teammates' 16 GB / 12 GB cards could run only a 4-bit quantized version, slowly, and those teammates proved unreliable. A pure CPU programmatic agent (state graph plus exploration, like the preview's "Blind Squirrel") is feasible without a GPU. But published programmatic agents score about 0.3-2.6 on the LB (github.com/Shih-Yu-Yeh/arc3-dev-agi-journal and others found in search), well below the 5+ that bronze likely needs (estimate). Conclusion: a medal-level entry needs a fork of the public LLM agent plus a few 9 h GPU runs. That fits the quota for a fork-and-tweak attempt. It does not fit real research: ranks 1-2 score 40+ and would need hundreds of GPU-h of iteration (estimate).
medal_chance: ESTIMATE, based on LB snapshot figures quoted in the task (2026-09-30) and Kaggle's medal thresholds for 1,000+ teams. With 3,493 teams, bronze is the top 10% (about rank 349), silver the top 5% (about rank 175), and gold roughly the top 17. The best public notebook scores 5.75 and sits at about rank 47. Over the last 33 days many teams will submit forks of the 5.75, 5.19 and 4.5 notebooks, so the bronze cutoff will probably settle near the best public notebook score, around 4-6. Estimated chances: bronze about 30% if we fork the best public agent and add a small, genuine improvement; silver about 5-8%; gold about 0%. These odds depend on the private half (55 unseen games) not reordering the cluster of forks at random. A pure fork with no improvement is closer to a coin flip for bronze, perhaps 20-25% (estimate).
summary: ARC-AGI-3 means building an agent that discovers the rules of hidden interactive grid games and solves them with about as few actions as humans need. It is a research problem, not a data-science one. The Milestone 1 winners (arcprize.org blog) all used locally hosted 27-31B LLMs: Qwen 3.6 27B writing code in a REPL, or Gemma-4-31B choosing actions from board images. They reported that simpler setups beat hand-crafted tool machinery. Our experience (3D microscopy, tracking, detection heads, GBM) barely transfers. Honest CV is impossible beyond the 25 public games: the preview winner StochasticGoose went from 12.58% on known games to 0.25% on the full unseen benchmark (arcprize.org/blog/arc-agi-3-preview-30-day-learnings). We also cannot iterate on an LLM agent without a GPU. On the other hand, the medal bar is unusually low for its position: the best public notebook (5.75) sits at about rank 47 of 3,493. A cheap fork plus a small tweak therefore has a real but fragile bronze chance (estimate about 30%). Recommendation: at most a low-effort side bet of about 1-2 person-weeks, capped at about 3-5 GPU runs. It should not be our main competition, because it breaks all three lessons: there is no honest CV, it is mostly knob-tuning of a public notebook rather than trained models, and we would be starting late. Fit 4/10.
dealbreakers: 1) There is no honest held-out CV. Only 25 public games exist, the 110 hidden games are different, and the previous competition showed a 50x collapse from known to unseen games. This is exactly the public-overfit trap the post-mortem warns about: tuned gains shrank about 5x on private. 2) Each evaluation is a ~9 h GPU notebook run. Assuming these runs draw on our ~30 GPU-h/week quota (not verified), we get about 3 runs a week, and there is no local GPU for fast iteration on a 27B LLM. 3) It is a novel research area where the top two (45.3 and 40.8) are ~7x ahead, so only bronze, and maybe silver, is realistic, and only by forking. 4) We would start late: 33 days left, with the entry and merger deadline on 2026-10-26. 5) Results are stochastic: LLM sampling plus only 55 private games means a fork cluster of hundreds of teams could reorder at random. Not strictly a dealbreaker: the winners must open-source their solutions, which matters only for prize ranks.
plan_first_2_weeks: Days 1-2, CPU only. Read the rules and the 3 top public notebooks (Affectify "Duck plus ours" 5.75, taaf-flashnext 5.19, Duck Qwen3.8 Tuned 4.5). Install the ARC-AGI-3-Agents repo locally and run the random agent on the 25 public games. Build a local scorer that reproduces the metric per level: min(h/a,1)^2, level-weighted. Days 3-4: fork the 5.75 notebook unchanged and do one 9 h run on the RTX 6000 or a Kaggle GPU. Submitting and accepting the rules need the user's approval. The run also shows us the real GPU-quota cost and the run-to-run variance. Days 5-9, CPU work. Add cheap, general, not game-specific improvements: detect dead or no-op actions and loops by state hashing (Blind Squirrel style), deduplicate clicks on the same object, and a stricter per-level action budget and reset policy that avoids wasting actions. The metric penalises extra actions quadratically. Validate these changes as leave-games-out on the 25 public games by replaying logged trajectories on CPU where possible. Days 10-14: at most 2 GPU runs of the best variant. Pick the final by agreement between the local 25-game score and the LB, never by the LB alone. Kill criterion: if by day 14 we are not clearly above the best public fork on the LB, stop and move effort to a better-fitting competition.
shakeup_risk: High. The private set is 55 unseen games (/data), and the per-game score is steep and quadratic in action efficiency. LLM agents are stochastic between runs. Hundreds of forks of the same 2-3 public agents will cluster within about 1 point near the bronze line, so their order on private is close to random (estimate). There is precedent: StochasticGoose's score collapsed on unseen games in the 2025 preview.
time_fit: Poor. 33 days remain, with entry and team merger closing on 2026-10-26 and the final deadline on 2026-11-02 at 23:59 UTC (/overview). That is enough for a fork-and-tweak bronze attempt, but not for the lessons we set ourselves. Start-early is violated. Honest CV cannot be built. And three months of accumulated GPU quota, which the post-mortem named as the real lever, is not available: about 4.5 weeks x 30 h is roughly 135 GPU-h at most, i.e. about 15 nine-hour runs, some of them spent on debugging.
skill_fit: Low. Of our experience, only pipeline and ops automation (notebook builder, run orchestration, local scorer) and AI-assisted coding transfer. 3D microscopy, tracking, detection heads and GBM are irrelevant. Prompt and agent-loop engineering is closer to what an AI coding assistant does well, but developing it properly requires LLM inference we cannot run locally. A CPU programmatic explorer is buildable, but the published ones score far below the bronze line.

compute_need:
A serious own model needs Kaggle GPU, not CPU. The data is 569.76 GB of DICOM (/data page). It cannot be downloaded to the laptop and has to be processed inside Kaggle notebooks, first as a one-off downsampling to a PNG or NPY dataset under 20 GB. That preprocessing is about 5-10 notebook-hours (estimate). Its time goes to CPU or I/O, but it runs in a 9-12 h session.

A public write-up of a 2D EfficientNet-B3 multiple-instance model (5-fold, 8 epochs) reports about 12.4 h of training, which lands at about 0.903 public (https://huggingface.co/blog/bishnoiyash/rsna-competetion, 9 Aug 2026). Today's top 50 are at 0.953-0.961 (leaderboard, 30 Sep). Reaching them takes several 2.5D/3D backbones per plane, multi-seed and blended, plus LLM label extraction from multilingual reports. For 3 weeks that comes to roughly 60-150+ GPU-h (estimate, based on the RSNA 2024 lumbar spine winners' multi-stage 2.5D pipelines). We have about 60-90 Kaggle GPU-h in the 22 days left (3 weeks of about 30 h), so we cannot match that.

A fork-and-blend of public notebooks needs only a few GPU-h per submission. Inference must fit within 9 h.
medal_chance:
These are estimates, not measurements.

- **Bronze: about 15-20%.** Bronze is about the top 10% of 4,618 teams, so around rank 462. Its public cutoff is probably 0.946-0.948: rank 49 is 0.953, and many CoAtNet/D4 forks sit at 0.943-0.945 (/leaderboard and /code, 30 Sep). The realistic route is a blend of public notebooks (best 0.946) plus one own Kaggle-trained head, landing around the cutoff. A shakeup could move us either way.
- **Silver: about 3%.** Silver is about the top 5%, around rank 231, which needs roughly 0.950-0.952 public (estimate). That requires own multi-model training we cannot do in 22 days.
- **Gold: about 0%.**

The basis is the leaderboard density quoted above plus our Biohub experience: public-LB-tuned gains shrank about 5x on private.

Mostly CPU. The core pipeline is: neutral-mass and formula candidate generation from a structure pool (training structures, COCONUT and a mass-indexed PubChem subset), spectral-similarity channels (entropy or modified cosine against 2.5M training spectra), fragmentation-explanation features, then a gradient-boosted LambdaRank ranker. The whole thing trains and runs on a laptop with 3 GB of parquet plus RDKit. One public repo (github.com/shiferaxa/casmi26) uses exactly this four-channel design with a GBM ranker and needs no GPU apart from its spectrum-to-fingerprint transformer.

The GPU part is optional and bounded, and one account's Kaggle quota covers it. Estimates:
- 20-60 GPU-h to train a MIST- or transformer-style spectrum-to-fingerprint model on about 2.5M spectra, or to fine-tune one.
- A few GPU-h for DreaMS embedding inference.
- About 10.7 weeks at 30 h/week is roughly 320 GPU-h, so these fit with plenty of room.

De novo generation for class 3 (DiffMS, MADGEN) is GPU-heavy and scores very low: MADGEN reports 1.31% top-1 on MassSpecGym (openreview ICLR 2025). We skip it, or at most add a cheap analog or scaffold-edit generator.

Inference has to fit in a 9 h notebook with no internet. PubChem candidates must be pre-built offline as a public Kaggle dataset, which is allowed as public external data. Building it (mass-filtered PubChem, InChIKey14 dedup, fingerprints) is a one-off CPU job of several hours on the laptop (estimate). Teammates' GPUs are not needed.

summary:
This is the best-fitting kind of competition for our constraints, and I recommend entering it. It is a retrieval-and-ranking problem over tabular or array spectra. The winning path looks like a candidate pool (training structures + COCONUT + PubChem), several similarity and fragmentation evidence channels, and a GBM or small-head ranker. All of that trains on CPU, and at most one bounded Kaggle-GPU job is needed for a spectrum-to-fingerprint model.

There is a natural honest CV from day one: enveda-np-examples (250 natural products, 1,151 spectra, the only instrument-matched natural-product data). The three novelty classes can be simulated with masks: full visibility; the molecule's own spectra hidden; the structure removed from the candidate pool. A public repo (shiferaxa/casmi26) reports that validating on random held-out training structures predicted the wrong ranking of rankers compared with the board, while the np-examples masks tracked it. That is the same "honest CV" lesson from our post-mortem. A naive molecule-disjoint in-library CV gives about 0.87 MRR (github.com/mardhav-2008) against an LB of about 0.4, which shows how much class 2 and class 3 drive the score.

The upside over the 0.386 notebook ceiling is visible: #1 is at 0.464. It comes mainly from class-2 database retrieval, which is engineering plus a ranker, and is not GPU-bound. Class 3 (de novo) is close to unsolvable at the state of the art (about 1-2% top-1), so everyone scores near zero there. That levels the field in our favour.

Risks:
- No domain background.
- A noisy 130-molecule public LB.
- A hidden class mix.
- A large field of forkers.
- Offline preparation of PubChem data within the 9 h / no-internet limits.

Estimates: fit 8/10; bronze about 40-50%, silver about 15-20%.

Sources: Kaggle /overview, /data, /leaderboard and /code pages, as given in the task; https://github.com/shiferaxa/casmi26; https://github.com/ibnmarzuk/casmi26-molecule-id; https://github.com/mardhav-2008/Enveda_CASMI_2026_Solution; https://openreview.net/pdf/6edc9aac27c89b06672fd3d16efbaa1dc13b9f96.pdf (MADGEN de novo accuracy).
shakeup_risk:
Moderate to high for anyone tuning to the public LB; lower for a CV-driven pipeline.
- The public split is about 33% of about 400 molecules, so roughly 130 molecules (/leaderboard banner). Per-molecule reciprocal rank is close to binary, so its SD is about 0.4-0.45. That makes the public MRR standard error about 0.035-0.04, and the private one (about 270 molecules) about 0.025 (estimate).
- The whole 0.383-0.401 plateau from rank 10 to 49 is therefore inside the noise. Public-LB tweaks will shrink or reverse on private, as happened in Biohub, where public gains shrank about 5x.
- The class mix is hidden and could differ between the public and private splits. A team heavy on class 1 could drop if private has more class-2 molecules.

Mitigations:
- Rank decisions on the np-examples three-mask CV.
- Keep one CV-best final and one robust or diverse final.
- Treat public LB moves under about 0.02 as noise.

- Per-candidate features: library similarity (max and top-k), analog Tanimoto to structures whose spectra match, mass error, formula plausibility, prior (PubChem reference count, NP-likeness), fraction of intensity explained by fragments.

Days 13-14
- Launch one Kaggle-GPU job: a spectrum-to-fingerprint model (MIST-style, or DreaMS embeddings plus an MLP head) as an extra ranker feature.

It is the rare competition where our binding constraint (GPU) matters less: the realistic lever is harness, prompt and skill engineering, which is CPU and code work that suits an AI assistant well. LoRA on a 31B model is out of reach for our compute, and per one unverified dev repo it may be ignored by the scorer anyway. Two things work against it. First, measurement is expensive: every honest CV pass needs the 31B model on Kaggle T4s, about 8-12 GPU-h for the 129 train tasks (estimate). Second, the score is extremely coarse. Verdict (estimate): a reasonable secondary bet or learning project, alongside a primary competition that suits CPU/GBM work. It should not be our main medal path. At p = 0.15 and n = 60, the binomial standard error is sqrt(0.15*0.85/60) = 0.046, about 2.8 tasks. On the 2026-09-30 board, one task (about 1.7 points) separates #1 from #2-#6, and #7-#25 are tied. Public and private are different task sets, possibly from different private repos, plus sampling nondeterminism. Expect rank swings of hundreds of places between public and private for mid-pack teams (estimate). Our past 5x shrink of public-tuned gains will probably be worse here. Mitigations: never tune on public; accept a change only if it wins by at least 2 SE on a held-out-repo CV with repeats; pick the final submission by CV plus robustness (e.g. whether the agent always produces a syntactically valid patch), not by public rank.

plan_first_2_weeks: Days 1-2: The user reads and accepts the rules manually (we do not join). Download the data only after that decision, and the user downloads it. Install the official harness (swegemma / adk-submission, versions per /data) under WSL2/Docker. Sanity check: gold patches should pass on the 129 train tasks on CPU. One dev repo reports 109/129 passing with gold, so identify and exclude the broken tasks. Days 2-4: Choose the serving path. (a) Kaggle T4 x2 notebook with llama.cpp Q4_0 or vLLM: measure tok/s, turns per task and the per-task wall-clock time within the 12 h / about 120-task budget. (b) Hosted Gemma 4 31B API for cheap iteration: run the same 30 tasks both ways, and adopt the API as a dev proxy only if the solve sets agree well. Freeze the CV: leave-one-repo-out, or a fixed 40-task holdout stratified by repo, plus 2 repeats per config to measure run-to-run noise. Write the acceptance rule: a change must beat baseline by at least 2 SE on the holdout. Days 4-7: Reproduce the best public notebook (0.15 LB) on our CV, and make ONE submission to calibrate CV against LB. Build a failure taxonomy from trajectories: wrong file localized, context overflow at 32k, patch not applied, tests not run, timeout. Week 2: Build CPU-side skills, each ablated on CV: (1) a localization skill combining BM25 over issue text, the provided embeddings and get_code_neighbors, returning a short ranked file/function list; (2) tool-output truncation and summarisation to protect the 32k context; (3) a reproduce-then-fix loop that writes a failing test from the issue, then runs targeted tests; (4) a patch guard (apply check, py_compile, run the nearest existing tests) with bounded retries; (5) a per-task time/turn budget controller so no task starves the 12 h run. End of week 2, go/no-go: continue only if CV is clearly above the public-notebook baseline by more than noise. Decide on LoRA only after verifying adapters are actually applied at scoring (a controlled probe, with user approval for the submission) and securing about 20-50 h of 80 GB-class GPU (estimate; rented, since teammates are unreliable). Otherwise stay harness-only and keep this as the secondary competition.
